 Advertisement Judge orders 30-year prison sentence for key figure in Minnesota food fraud
 Advertisement Updated: 4:41 PM EDT Oct 28, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ The Associated Press Judge orders 30-year prison sentence for key figure in Minnesota food fraud
 Updated: 4:41 PM EDT Oct 28, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ The Associated Press MINNEAPOLIS — A man who played a major role in defrauding a federal food program in Minnesota was sentenced Wednesday to 30 years in prison, the latest punishment in a sprawling scheme to collect millions of dollars during the COVID-19 pandemic by claiming to have fed needy children.
 Video above: Trump announces $25 million whistleblower program for alleged government fraud 
 Advertisement The depth of fraud in Minnesota — dozens of people have been convicted — has repeatedly drawn the attention of President Donald Trump, who ridiculed the Democratic governor for failing to stop it and partly cited it as grounds for a massive immigration crackdown in the state's largest cities.
 Salim Said operated Safari Restaurant in Minneapolis, which specialized in dishes from Somalia. He was accused of vastly overstating the number of meals when seeking payment for providing food. The government said he was responsible for $44 million in fraud, some of which was committed by others he recruited.
 “You took more than taxpayers' dollars to enrich yourself. You took the reputation of our state down with you,” U.S. District Judge Nancy Brasel said.
 Said was claiming a “ridiculous daily distribution of 6,000 meals” while FBI cameras showed 40 people a day collecting food, prosecutors said in a court filing.
 “The defendant and his sites did not serve thousands of children; he served a calculated, lucrative lie,” prosecutors said.
 Nonprofit leader at center of sprawling Minnesota fraud case gets nearly 42-year prison sentence Said, a native of Somalia, denied the allegations while testifying at the trial in 2025, saying many meals were delivered off-site. But at his sentencing Wednesday, he changed course and expressed remorse. Defense attorney Barry Zone, who had asked for a 12-year prison sentence, disputed that Said was the “architect” as the government alleged.
 COVID-19 brought changes to a federal program that typically fed children through schools. Restaurants could participate, and food distribution was extended to places outside schools.
 “For 21 consecutive months, Said made thousands of fraudulent reimbursement claims, day after day, month after month,” prosecutors said. “Each submission represented meals purportedly provided to underprivileged children, yet the listed children themselves were entirely fictitious.”
 The government said Said hit the jackpot: He bought a $1.2 million home, commercial real estate and an $87,000 pickup truck.
 Said was convicted of a raft of charges in 2025, along with Aimee Bock , the leader of a Minnesota nonprofit, Feeding Our Future. She is serving a 42-year prison sentence for devising the overall plan to recruit Said and others to join the federal food program during the pandemic.
 State auditors found that the Minnesota Department of Education received numerous complaints about Feeding Our Future, but often told the group to police itself. In January, Gov. Tim Walz said he would not run for reelection after being pounded by Trump about theft in programs that rely on federal cash.
